### Title: Code on the Combine: Right to Repair and Agricultural Telemetry Monopolies

Modern farming equipment is no longer purely mechanical; a contemporary combine harvester contains over a hundred electronic control units (ECUs) running millions of lines of proprietary code. Companies like John Deere have utilized this digital transformation to fundamentally redefine farm machinery ownership. Through software locks, digital rights management (DRM), and restrictive end-user license agreements (EULAs), manufacturers have monopolized diagnostic and repair services, creating severe economic and operational bottlenecks for independent farmers.

Under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) Section 1201, circumventing a technological measure that controls access to a copyrighted work is illegal. Manufacturers argue that tractor firmware is proprietary copyrighted code, meaning that an independent mechanic or farmer who uses third-party diagnostic software to calibrate a replaced hydraulic sensor is committing copyright infringement. When a tractor fails during critical planting or harvesting windows—where delays of 48 hours can result in tens of thousands of dollars in ruined crops—farmers cannot repair their own machines. They are legally and technically compelled to wait for an authorized dealership technician carrying a proprietary diagnostic software tool (such as Deere's 'Service ADVISOR') to enter a software authorization code.

The manufacturer's standard defense is that closed software ecosystems protect operator safety and emissions compliance. They argue that open diagnostics would allow farmers to override EPA-mandated Tier 4 emissions controls or bypass safety interlocks. However, this argument conflates diagnostic access with unauthorized modification. State-level Right to Repair legislation (such as Colorado's Consumer Right to Repair Agricultural Equipment Act of 2023) specifically requires manufacturers to provide parts, diagnostic tools, and software documentation at fair and reasonable terms without requiring disclosure of underlying source code or emissions-override tools.

This battle is not simply about mechanics; it is about whether intellectual property law can be weaponized to turn tangible capital goods into rent-generating digital enclosures. When farmers lose the ability to repair their own tools, agricultural independence is replaced by platform feudalism.
